title: Transformations and the Pythagorean Theorem
bigQuestion: What stays the same when a shape slides, flips, turns or grows, and how does a right angle connect three lengths?

story.title: A 3-4-5 Rope and the Builders of the Pyramids
story.kicker: A knotted rope, twelve equal spaces and three people pulling can make a perfect right angle without any tool at all.
paragraphs: Take a rope and tie twelve knots in it, all the same distance apart, and then tie the ends together so the knots form a loop of twelve equal spaces. Hand it to three friends. The first holds a knot. The second walks three spaces along the rope and pulls it tight. The third walks four more spaces and pulls tight, so that the last five spaces stretch back to the first person. When all three pull, the rope forms a triangle with sides of 3, 4 and 5 spaces. The corner between the 3 side and the 4 side is a perfect right angle. Every time.

Many books tell of ancient Egyptian rope stretchers who laid out fields and temple foundations with cords like this after the Nile flooded each year and washed away the boundary markers. Historians are not certain the Egyptians used the 3-4-5 rope for right angles, but rope stretchers did exist, and the trick itself works whether or not they knew it. What is certain is that people knew special triangles long before anyone wrote down a proof.

A clay tablet from ancient Babylon, made more than a thousand years before the Greek mathematician Pythagoras was born, lists sets of three whole numbers where the squares of the first two add up to the square of the third. 3, 4 and 5 is the simplest: 9 + 16 = 25. Another is 5, 12 and 13: 25 + 144 = 169. The Babylonians knew the pattern. The Greeks later proved why it must hold for every right triangle, and the rule carries the name of Pythagoras today.

The rule says: in any right triangle, the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. It is why a carpenter checks a corner by measuring 3 feet along one board and 4 feet along the other and looking for exactly 5 feet across. It is why a ladder of a known length reaches a height you can calculate. It is how a phone finds the straight-line distance between two spots on a map.

This chapter has two parts that fit together. First, you will move shapes: slide them, flip them, turn them, and stretch them, and see which measurements survive each move. Then you will meet the right-triangle rule, prove it by cutting up squares, and use it to measure distances that no ruler can reach.
story.think: The rope trick needs twelve equal spaces. Why would a loop with ten spaces, split 3-3-4, not give a right angle? What would you check?

lessons.title: Sliding: Translations
lessons.mainIdea: A translation slides every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction, so the image is an exact copy in a new place.
reading: Slide a book across a table without turning it. Every corner of the book moves the same distance in the same direction. That move is a *translation*. The moved shape is called the *image*, and it is the same size and shape as the original, just somewhere else. On a coordinate grid, a translation is a rule like: add 3 to every x and subtract 2 from every y.

Take a triangle with corners at A(0, 0), B(3, 0) and C(0, 4). Translate it 2 units right and 1 unit up. Add 2 to each x and 1 to each y. A goes to A'(2, 1), B goes to B'(5, 1), and C goes to C'(2, 5). The little mark after each letter is read 'A prime' and means the image of A. The new triangle has the same side lengths and the same angles as the old one.

Directions turn into signs. Right means add to x, left means subtract from x. Up means add to y, down means subtract from y. The point (−2, 5) moved 4 right and 3 down becomes (−2 + 4, 5 − 3) = (2, 2). Moving left 4 and up 3 instead would give (−6, 8).

The most common mistake is mixing the signs, adding when you should subtract. Another is applying the rule to only one corner. Every point must move by the same amounts, or the shape stretches and it is no longer a translation. Check by comparing one side before and after: it should be the same length and point the same way.

words.d: a slide that moves every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction
the new shape you get after a transformation; its corners are named with a prime mark, like A'
a pair of numbers (x, y) that names a point's position on a grid

look.title: Moving the Couch
look.text: A floor plan of a living room is drawn on a grid. The couch is a rectangle with corners at (1, 1), (5, 1), (5, 3) and (1, 3). The family slides it 3 units to the right and 2 units up, without turning it, to make room for a table.
look.prompt: Write the four new corner coordinates. Is the couch still 4 units wide and 2 units deep?

check.q: The point (−2, 5) is translated 4 units right and 3 units down. Where does it land?
check.why: Right adds to x, down subtracts from y: (−2 + 4, 5 − 3) = (2, 2).

check.q: A triangle has corners A(0, 0), B(3, 0) and C(0, 4). After a translation 2 right and 1 up, where is C'?
After a translation, what is true about the image compared with the original shape?
choices: It is the same size and shape, facing the same way
check.why: A slide moves every point the same way, so lengths, angles and the direction the shape faces do not change.

lessons.title: Flipping: Reflections
lessons.mainIdea: A reflection flips a shape across a line, so the image is a mirror copy the same distance from the line on the other side.
reading: Hold a letter up to a mirror. The mirror image is the same size, but left and right are swapped. That is a *reflection*, and the mirror is the *line of reflection*. Every point of the image is exactly as far from the line as the original point, but on the opposite side. If a point sits on the line itself, it does not move at all.

On the coordinate grid, the two easiest mirrors are the axes. Reflecting across the *x-axis* flips the shape up to down: the x stays and the y changes sign. The point (3, −2) becomes (3, 2). Reflecting across the y-axis flips left to right: the y stays and the x changes sign. The point (3, −2) becomes (−3, −2).

Try a whole triangle: corners at (1, 1), (4, 1) and (1, 3). Reflect across the y-axis: (−1, 1), (−4, 1) and (−1, 3). The image is the same size, and every side is the same length. But a corner that used to be on the left is now on the right. If you read the corners going around, the direction reverses, like a clock running backward.

Watch which coordinate changes. Students often flip the wrong one. Think about what the mirror does. The x-axis is a horizontal line, so a flip across it moves points up or down, which is a change in y. The y-axis is vertical, so a flip across it moves points left or right, which is a change in x.

words.d: a flip across a line that makes a mirror image the same distance from the line on the other side
the mirror line; every point and its image are the same distance from it
the horizontal number line on a grid, where y is 0

look.title: Mirror on the Wall
look.text: A dance studio has a mirror running along the y-axis of a grid painted on the floor. A dancer stands at (5, 2). Her friend stands at (2, −3). A third dancer stands right at the mirror, at (0, 4). Each looks at her own reflection in the mirror.
look.prompt: Give the coordinates of each reflection. Which dancer's reflection is at the same spot she is?

check.q: The point (3, −2) is reflected across the x-axis. Where is its image?
check.why: Flipping across the horizontal axis changes the sign of y only: (3, 2).

check.q: The point (3, −2) is reflected across the y-axis. Where is its image?
check.why: Flipping across the vertical axis changes the sign of x only: (−3, −2).

check.q: Which statement about a reflection is true?
choices: The image is smaller than the original
A point on the line of reflection does not move
Every point moves the same distance
The image faces the same way as the original
check.why: Points on the mirror line stay put. Other points move to the opposite side, and the image is a mirror copy that faces the opposite way.

lessons.title: Turning: Rotations
lessons.mainIdea: A rotation turns a shape around a fixed center point by a set angle, and every point stays the same distance from that center.
reading: Pin one corner of a paper triangle to a board and spin the paper. That is a *rotation*. The pin is the *center of rotation*, and the amount of spin is the angle, such as 90 or 180 degrees. Counterclockwise is the usual direction unless a problem says clockwise. Every point stays exactly as far from the center as it was; it just swings to a new spot.

On the grid, rotating about the origin has simple rules. A 90-degree counterclockwise turn sends (x, y) to (−y, x). So (4, 1) goes to (−1, 4). A 180-degree turn sends (x, y) to (−x, −y), so (4, 1) goes to (−4, −1). A 90-degree clockwise turn sends (x, y) to (y, −x), so (4, 1) goes to (1, −4). The distance from the origin never changes: the point (4, 1) and all three images are the same distance from (0, 0).

You can check a 90-degree turn with a picture. From the origin, go 4 right and 1 up to reach (4, 1). Turn that path a quarter turn counterclockwise: right becomes up and up becomes left. Now go 4 up and 1 left, which is (−1, 4). It matches the rule.

The rule for 90 degrees is the one students mix up most. The coordinates swap and one of them changes sign. Which one? For counterclockwise, the new x is the negative of the old y. Test it with a point you can picture: (1, 0) on the right side of the grid should turn to (0, 1) at the top, and the rule gives (−0, 1) = (0, 1).

words.d: a turn around a fixed center point by a set angle
the point that stays still while everything else turns around it
turning in the direction opposite to a clock's hands

look.title: The Ferris Wheel Seat
look.text: A Ferris wheel is drawn on a grid with its center at the origin. A seat starts at (0, −10), the very bottom. The wheel turns counterclockwise. After a quarter turn the seat is on one side; after a half turn it is at the top; after three quarters of a turn it is on the other side.
look.prompt: Give the seat's coordinates after 90, 180 and 270 degrees. How far is the seat from the center each time?

check.q: The point (4, 1) is rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin. Where is its image?
check.why: A 90-degree counterclockwise turn sends (x, y) to (−y, x): (−1, 4). (1, −4) is the clockwise turn.

check.q: The point (4, 1) is rotated 180 degrees about the origin. Where is its image?
check.why: A half turn changes both signs: (−4, −1).

check.q: A point is 5 units from the center of rotation. After a 90-degree rotation, how far is its image from the center?
check.why: Rotation keeps every point the same distance from the center. The point swings but does not move closer or farther.

lessons.title: Growing: Dilations
lessons.mainIdea: A dilation multiplies every distance from a center by a scale factor, changing the size of a shape but not its shape.
reading: A projector throws a small image onto a big screen. Every length gets multiplied by the same number, and every angle stays exactly the same. That is a *dilation*. It has a center, the point the shape grows out from, and a scale factor. A scale factor bigger than 1 enlarges; a scale factor between 0 and 1 shrinks.

On the grid with the center at the origin, the rule is easy: multiply both coordinates by the scale factor. With scale factor 2, the point (2, 3) becomes (4, 6). With scale factor 3, the point (3, −1) becomes (9, −3). With scale factor 1/2, the point (8, 6) becomes (4, 3). A triangle with corners (0, 0), (2, 0) and (0, 1) dilated by 3 becomes (0, 0), (6, 0) and (0, 3): three times as wide and three times as tall.

Unlike slides, flips and turns, a dilation changes lengths. Every side of the image is the scale factor times the matching side of the original. But it does not change angles, and it does not change the shape. A dilated square is still a square. A dilated triangle has the same three angles as before.

Two mistakes to avoid. One is adding the scale factor instead of multiplying: (3, −1) with scale factor 3 is (9, −3), not (6, 2). The other is scaling only one coordinate, which stretches the shape in one direction and ruins its angles. Both coordinates get multiplied, every time.

words.d: a transformation that enlarges or shrinks a shape by multiplying every distance from a center by a scale factor
the point (0, 0) where the x-axis and y-axis cross

look.title: One Point, Many Scale Factors
look.cite: Dilations centered at the origin: (x, y) becomes (kx, ky)
look.prompt: Write the full image point, with both coordinates, for each scale factor. Which scale factor leaves the point where it is?

check.q: The point (3, −1) is dilated from the origin with scale factor 3. Where is its image?
check.why: Multiply both coordinates by 3: (9, −3). Adding 3 gives (6, 2), which is wrong.

check.q: The point (8, 6) is dilated from the origin with scale factor 1/2. Where is its image?
check.why: Half of each coordinate: (4, 3).

check.q: What does a dilation change, and what does it keep?
check.why: Every length is multiplied by the scale factor, but the shape and its angles stay the same.

lessons.title: Congruent or Similar
lessons.mainIdea: Two shapes are congruent if slides, flips and turns can lay one exactly on the other, and similar if a dilation is also allowed.
reading: Two shapes are *congruent* when they are the same shape and the same size, so one could be laid exactly on top of the other. In terms of moves: two shapes are congruent if some sequence of translations, reflections and rotations carries one onto the other. Those three moves never change lengths or angles, so they are called *rigid motions*. A triangle and its image after a rotation are always congruent.

Two shapes are *similar* when they have the same shape but maybe a different size. In terms of moves: two shapes are similar if rigid motions plus a dilation carry one onto the other. A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 and a triangle with sides 6, 8 and 10 are similar. Divide the matching sides: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, 8 ÷ 4 = 2, 10 ÷ 5 = 2. The scale factor is 2 for every pair, and the angles match.

To test for similarity, divide every pair of matching sides and see if you get the same number each time. A 2 by 3 rectangle and a 4 by 5 rectangle are not similar, because 4 ÷ 2 = 2 but 5 ÷ 3 is not 2. The second one is stretched more one way than the other. A 2 by 3 rectangle and a 4 by 6 rectangle are similar, with scale factor 2.

Every congruent pair is also similar, with scale factor 1. But similar shapes are not always congruent. A student who says two triangles are congruent just because their angles match has forgotten about size. Angles alone prove similarity; you need matching side lengths to prove congruence.

words.d: the same shape and the same size; one can be moved to fit exactly on the other
the same shape, possibly a different size; matching angles are equal and matching sides share one scale factor
a translation, reflection or rotation; a move that keeps every length and angle

look.title: Phone Screens
look.text: Three phones are on a table. The first has a screen 6 cm wide and 13 cm tall. The second has a screen 7.2 cm wide and 15.6 cm tall. The third has a screen 6 cm wide and 13 cm tall but is turned sideways. A student wants to know which screens are congruent, which are similar and which are neither.
look.prompt: Divide matching sides to decide. Which pairs are congruent? Which are similar but not congruent?

check.q: Which pair of shapes must be congruent?
choices: A triangle and its image after a rotation
A triangle and its image after a dilation by 2
check.why: A rotation is a rigid motion, so it keeps every length and angle. The image fits exactly on the original.

check.q: A triangle has sides 3, 4 and 5. Another has sides 6, 8 and 10. What is their relationship?
check.why: 6 ÷ 3, 8 ÷ 4 and 10 ÷ 5 all equal 2, so the shapes match with scale factor 2. Different sizes, so not congruent.

check.q: Is a 2 by 3 rectangle similar to a 4 by 5 rectangle?
check.why: Similar shapes need the same scale factor on every pair of sides. Here the ratios differ, so the shapes are stretched differently.

lessons.title: Squares on a Right Triangle
lessons.mainIdea: In a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a² + b² = c², and you can prove it by fitting four copies of the triangle inside a square.
reading: In a right triangle, the two sides that form the right angle are the *legs*. The third side, across from the right angle, is the *hypotenuse*, and it is always the longest. Call the legs a and b and the hypotenuse c. The *Pythagorean theorem* says a² + b² = c². For the 3-4-5 triangle, the legs are 3 and 4, so 9 + 16 = 25, and 25 = 5². It works.

Here is a proof by areas. Draw a big square with sides of length a + b. Inside it, place four copies of the right triangle, one in each corner, each with its legs along the edges. The four hypotenuses form a tilted square in the middle with side c. Now count the area two ways. The big square has area (a + b)², which multiplies out to a² + 2ab + b². The four triangles together have area 4 × (1/2 × a × b) = 2ab, and the tilted square has area c². So a² + 2ab + b² = 2ab + c². Take 2ab from both sides: a² + b² = c².

Use it to find a hypotenuse. Legs 5 and 12: 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169. The hypotenuse is the number that squares to 169, which is 13, because 13 × 13 = 169. Legs 8 and 15: 64 + 225 = 289 = 17², so the hypotenuse is 17. Legs 6 and 8: 36 + 64 = 100, so 10.

The classic mistake is adding the legs instead of their squares: 5 + 12 = 17 is wrong; the hypotenuse is 13. Another is forgetting to take the square root at the end and answering 169. A third is using the theorem on a triangle that has no right angle, where it simply does not apply.

words.d: the longest side of a right triangle, across from the right angle
the two sides of a right triangle that meet at the right angle
in a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a² + b² = c²
the number that multiplies by itself to give another; √169 = 13 because 13 × 13 = 169

look.title: Whole-Number Right Triangles
look.cite: Pythagorean triples: whole numbers with a² + b² = c²
look.prompt: Check two rows by squaring and adding. The 6-8-10 row is the 3-4-5 row doubled; what would 9-12-? be?

check.q: A right triangle has legs of 5 cm and 12 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
check.why: 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169, and √169 = 13 cm. Adding the legs gives 17, which is wrong.

check.q: In the proof with four triangles inside a square of side a + b, why does a² + b² = c² follow?
choices: Because the triangles are all the same size
Because c is the longest side
Because a² + 2ab + b² = 2ab + c², and 2ab cancels from both sides
Because the big square has four corners
check.why: Both sides count the same big square's area. Removing the four triangles' area, 2ab, leaves a² + b² on one side and c² on the other.

check.q: Which side of a right triangle is the hypotenuse?
choices: Either side that touches the right angle
The side across from the right angle, always the longest
check.why: The hypotenuse faces the right angle and is longer than either leg. Position on the page does not matter.

lessons.title: Finding a Missing Side
lessons.mainIdea: To find a leg, subtract the other leg's square from the hypotenuse's square; to find the hypotenuse, add the squares of the legs.
reading: The theorem finds any one side from the other two. If the hypotenuse is missing, add: c² = a² + b². If a leg is missing, subtract: a² = c² − b². The hypotenuse is always the biggest, so its square goes alone on one side of the equation.

A right triangle has hypotenuse 10 and one leg 6. The other leg: 10² − 6² = 100 − 36 = 64, and √64 = 8. Check: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10². Another: hypotenuse 15, leg 9. Then 225 − 81 = 144, and √144 = 12. A student who adds instead of subtracting gets 225 + 81 = 306 and √306, which is about 17.5, longer than the hypotenuse. That is impossible, so an answer longer than the hypotenuse is a signal to go back.

Not every answer is a whole number. Legs 2 and 3 give 4 + 9 = 13, and √13 is not a whole number. It is between √9 = 3 and √16 = 4, closer to 3.6, because 3.6 × 3.6 = 12.96. A calculator gives 3.606. Write the exact answer as √13 and the estimate as about 3.6.

Two habits protect you. First, label the hypotenuse before you write anything, so you know whether to add or subtract. Second, check your result by putting all three sides back into a² + b² = c². If the check fails, the error is usually a squared number or a sign.

words.d: a close but not exact value, like 3.6 for √13
a number that is a whole number times itself, like 64 = 8 × 8

look.title: The Kite String
look.text: A kite is flying on a string 25 meters long. The string is pulled tight and straight. The kite is directly above a spot on the ground that is 7 meters from where the child stands. The string, the ground and the vertical line down from the kite form a right triangle, with the string as the hypotenuse.
look.prompt: How high is the kite? Which side did you subtract, and how did you check?

check.q: A right triangle has hypotenuse 15 and one leg 9. What is the other leg?
check.why: 15² − 9² = 225 − 81 = 144, and √144 = 12. Adding instead gives about 17.5, which is longer than the hypotenuse.

check.q: A right triangle has legs 8 and 15. What is the hypotenuse?
A right triangle has legs 2 and 3. About how long is the hypotenuse?

lessons.title: Is It a Right Triangle?
lessons.mainIdea: The converse of the Pythagorean theorem says that if the three sides satisfy a² + b² = c², the triangle has a right angle.
reading: The theorem runs one way: a right triangle gives a² + b² = c². The *converse* runs the other way: if the three sides of a triangle satisfy a² + b² = c², with c the longest, then the angle across from c is a right angle. That is why the 3-4-5 rope works. 9 + 16 = 25, so the corner between the 3 and the 4 must be square.

To test a triangle, square the two shorter sides and add them, then compare with the square of the longest side. Sides 7, 24 and 25: 49 + 576 = 625, and 25² = 625. Equal, so it is a right triangle. Sides 4, 5 and 6: 16 + 25 = 41, but 6² = 36. Not equal, so no right angle. Sides 9, 12 and 15: 81 + 144 = 225 = 15². Right triangle.

The comparison also tells you what kind of triangle you have. If a² + b² is greater than c², the largest angle is less than 90 degrees, and the triangle is acute. If a² + b² is less than c², the largest angle is more than 90 degrees, and the triangle is obtuse. For 4, 5 and 6, 41 is more than 36, so the triangle is acute.

Builders use the converse every day. To check that a wall meets the floor at a right angle, mark 3 feet up the wall and 4 feet along the floor, then measure between the marks. Exactly 5 feet means square. More than 5 means the corner is too open; less means it is too tight. The common error is squaring the wrong side: c must be the longest, always.

words.d: a statement turned around: if the theorem says A leads to B, the converse says B leads to A
an angle bigger than 90 degrees, or a triangle that has one

look.title: Checking the Deck
look.text: A crew builds a rectangular deck. To check one corner, a carpenter measures 6 feet along one edge and 8 feet along the other and makes two marks. Then she measures the straight distance between the marks and gets 10 feet 2 inches. Her partner says the corner is fine because it looks square.
look.prompt: Is the corner a right angle? Is it too open or too tight? What should the distance be?

check.q: A triangle has sides 7, 24 and 25. Is it a right triangle?
choices: Yes, because all right triangles have a side of 25
check.why: The two shorter sides' squares add to the longest side's square, so the converse says the triangle has a right angle.

check.q: A triangle has sides 4, 5 and 6. Which is true?
choices: It is not a right triangle, because 16 + 25 = 41 and 6² = 36
It is a right triangle because 4 + 5 is more than 6
check.why: 41 is not equal to 36, so there is no right angle. Since 41 is greater than 36, the triangle is acute.

check.q: Which set of sides does NOT make a right triangle?
check.why: 7² + 8² = 49 + 64 = 113, but 9² = 81. The other three sets satisfy a² + b² = c².

lessons.title: Distance on a Grid
lessons.mainIdea: To find the distance between two points on a grid, draw the right triangle between them and use the Pythagorean theorem on its legs.
reading: Two points on a grid are usually not on the same row or column, so you cannot just count squares between them. But you can build a right triangle. From the first point go straight across, then straight up or down to the second point. The across distance and the up distance are the legs. The straight line between the points is the hypotenuse.

Find the distance from (1, 2) to (4, 6). Across: from x = 1 to x = 4 is 3. Up: from y = 2 to y = 6 is 4. Legs 3 and 4 make hypotenuse 5, so the distance is 5. Another: from (2, 1) to (7, 13). Across 7 − 2 = 5. Up 13 − 1 = 12. Distance √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13.

Negative coordinates work the same way; just be careful with the subtraction. From (−3, 2) to (3, 10): across is 3 − (−3) = 6, and up is 10 − 2 = 8. Distance √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10. If the answer is not a perfect square, estimate it. From (0, 0) to (2, 3): √(4 + 9) = √13, about 3.6.

The most common error is subtracting the wrong pairs, mixing an x with a y. Always subtract x from x and y from y. A second error is skipping the squares and adding the legs, which gives the walking distance along the grid lines, not the straight-line distance. The straight line is always shorter.

words.d: the length of the straight line between two points
the coordinate plane, marked in equal squares with an x-axis and a y-axis

look.title: The Drone Flight
look.text: A city map is drawn on a grid where each unit is 1 kilometer. A delivery drone takes off from a warehouse at (2, 3) and flies in a straight line to a customer at (8, 11). A truck making the same delivery has to drive along the streets: 6 blocks east, then 8 blocks north.
look.prompt: How far does the drone fly? How far does the truck drive? How much distance does the drone save?

check.q: What is the distance from (2, 1) to (7, 13)?
What is the distance from (−3, 2) to (3, 10)?
About what is the distance from (0, 0) to (2, 3)?
check.why: √(2² + 3²) = √13, which is about 3.6. Adding 2 + 3 = 5 gives the path along the grid lines, not the straight line.

lessons.title: Ladders, Screens and Diagonals
lessons.mainIdea: Whenever a real situation contains a right angle, the Pythagorean theorem can find a length that is hard to measure directly.
reading: A ladder leaning on a wall makes a right triangle: the wall is one leg, the ground is the other, and the ladder is the hypotenuse. A 13-foot ladder has its base 5 feet from the wall. How high does it reach? 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, and √144 = 12. It reaches 12 feet. A 10-foot ladder with its base 6 feet out reaches √(100 − 36) = √64 = 8 feet.

Television screens are sold by their diagonal, corner to corner. A screen 40 inches wide and 30 inches tall has diagonal √(1600 + 900) = √2500 = 50 inches. A widescreen 48 inches wide and 27 inches tall has diagonal √(2304 + 729) = √3033, about 55 inches, since 55² = 3025. That is why a '55-inch' TV is much less than 55 inches wide.

Diagonals also save steps. A rectangular park is 300 m by 400 m. Walking around two sides from one corner to the opposite corner is 300 + 400 = 700 m. Cutting straight across the diagonal is √(90,000 + 160,000) = √250,000 = 500 m. The shortcut saves 200 m. The same triangle at a different scale tells you whether a 3-meter pole fits diagonally in a 2 m by 2 m box: √8 is about 2.8, so it does not.

The skill is spotting the right angle. Walls meet floors at right angles. Screens and doors have square corners. North and east are perpendicular directions. Once you see the square corner, label the two legs and the hypotenuse, decide which one is missing, and then add or subtract the squares.

words.d: a straight line joining two opposite corners of a rectangle
a screen shape that is much wider than it is tall, common on TVs and laptops

look.title: Ladder Reach
rows: 13 ft ladder, base 5 ft from wall
10 ft ladder, base 6 ft from wall
15 ft ladder, base 9 ft from wall
17 ft ladder, base 8 ft from wall
25 ft ladder, base 7 ft from wall
26 ft ladder, base 10 ft from wall
look.prompt: Check the 17-foot row by squaring. Two ladders reach 12 feet; which one is at a steeper, safer angle, and how can you tell?

check.q: A 10-foot ladder has its base 6 feet from a wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
check.why: 10² − 6² = 100 − 36 = 64, and √64 = 8 feet. Adding the squares gives about 11.7, longer than the ladder.

check.q: A TV screen is 48 inches wide and 27 inches tall. About what is its diagonal?
A rectangular park is 300 m by 400 m. How much shorter is the diagonal path than walking around two sides?
check.why: Two sides: 700 m. Diagonal: √(300² + 400²) = 500 m. Savings: 700 − 500 = 200 m.

review.q: The point (5, −3) is translated 2 units left and 4 units up. Where is its image?
review.why: Left subtracts from x, up adds to y: (5 − 2, −3 + 4) = (3, 1).

review.q: The point (−4, 6) is reflected across the y-axis. Where is its image?
review.why: A flip across the vertical axis changes the sign of x only: (4, 6).

Which transformation can change the size of a shape?
review.why: Only a dilation multiplies lengths by a scale factor. The other three are rigid motions that keep every length.

A right triangle has hypotenuse 26 and one leg 10. What is the other leg?
review.why: 26² − 10² = 676 − 100 = 576, and √576 = 24. Adding instead gives √776, about 27.9, which is too long.

review.q: A triangle has sides 8, 15 and 17. Is it a right triangle?
choices: Yes, because all three sides are different
review.why: The squares of the two shorter sides add to the square of the longest, so the converse gives a right angle.
